https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r: Review scores for GTA 6 are a fairytale ending after years of development
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 , external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN , external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , external , but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times , external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
Critics say the relationship between Jason and Lucia is central to the game

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian , external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes , external , Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post , external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg , external 's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z0: Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language .
These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.
There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.
As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.
In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm87: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwq6: As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg: The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.
But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.
The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: The Australia playing squad and staff were pictured before the third Test against South Africa in 2018
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
TMS podcast: How does Bancroft's revelation impact 'sandpapergate'?
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United , will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.
Sunderland , wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.
But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.
Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.
In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.
That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.
Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.
This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.
The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.
This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.
Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.
Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.
While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.
Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.
Sunderland 's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.
In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.
Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Rassie Erasmus took the South Africa job after the departure of Allister Coetzee
Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.
Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.
The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.
It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.
Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence.
"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side.
"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"
Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.

Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching" , external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.
Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.
South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.
He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.
Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.
They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.

Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.
Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match.
He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.
Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.
There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off.
Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.
Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.
"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.
"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.
"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."
France's win over South Africa was only the Springboks' third defeat in 11 matches this year
But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.
But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.
Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.
However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term.
Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.
It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".

In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.
"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."

In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.

"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

However he has also said that the ability of European football associations to do so has been made harder by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin deciding to stand for a fourth term earlier this year. Ceferin reversed a previous insistence, in 2024, he would not seek re-election.

The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.
European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.

Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".

It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl: Luke Littler's title defence is over despite an average of 101.38 against Jermaine Wattimena
Defending champion Luke Littler suffered a shock early exit at the Grand Slam of Darts after a stunning display from Jermaine Wattimena.
The Dutchman was in tears after securing a remarkable, and thoroughly deserved, 10-8 victory in the second round in Wolverhampton.

Having looked imperious as he won six legs on the spin to take a 7-2 lead, 16th seed Wattimena showed signs of nerves as the finish line approached, but dug in to stave off a late Littler comeback and progress to the quarter-finals.
"I think I played really incredible, I played my best game on this stage and I'm really proud of it," an emotional Wattimena told Sky Sports.
"He started playing well at the end. Last leg, [I had] one dart for the match - amazing."

Wattimena finished with an average of 101.70 having hit a staggering 10 180s and, such was his level for the majority of the match, he might feel the margin of victory should have been more comfortable.
The 38-year-old twice threatened nine-darters and had two darts for an 8-2 lead, with Littler rarely even given a look at a double.
However, the 19-year-old world champion sensed an opportunity and showed his class with a 10-darter to break throw as Wattimena finally stuttered a leg from victory.
But a dramatic comeback fell just short as, with Littler waiting to pounce on 65, Wattimena hit tops to take out 77 for the match and reach the last eight of the tournament for a second time.
Wattimena will face compatriot Kevin Doets in the next round after the world number 23 saw off Scotland's Cameron Menzies 10-5.
Doets averaged 101.51 and matched Wattimena's 10 maximums as his relentless scoring made up for an off night on the doubles.
Jermaine Wattimena will face fellow Dutchman Kevin Doets in the next round
Fourth seed Gerwyn Price is also through after a clinical display to beat Englishman Ryan Searle 10-7.
The Welshman averaged 103.31 and hit 45% of his doubles to see off 13th seed Searle, who himself averaged just under 100.
Price will face Niko Springer for a place in the semi-finals after he overcame former world champion Rob Cross 10-8.
Cross averaged 96.05 to Springer's 88.59, but the German's finishing was far superior - with a checkout rate of 48% - and that proved the difference.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic: Lawyers for world number one Alexander Zverev say he will defend himself against a lawsuit which alleges he misrepresented the outcome of his domestic abuse trial.
Former partner Brenda Patea is seeking damages and an injunction against him making similar comments in future.
In October 2023 Zverev was issued with a penalty order for bodily harm against Patea, with whom he has a daughter.
He contested the order, having always denied the charges, and a public trial was under way in Berlin in June 2024 when the court terminated the proceedings.
"The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence," the court told the BBC.
"One decisive factor for the decision was that the witness has expressed her wish to end the trial. The defendant agreed to the termination of the case."
The court said there had been a separate settlement between Zverev and Patea.

But in September - as first reported by the Bounces website - lawyers for Patea filed a civil complaint in Berlin about an interview Zverev gave to French newspaper L'Equipe in June the day after he won his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros.
According to the complaint, L'Equipe reported that Zverev allegedly said "my innocence has been proven".

The lawsuit asks that Zverev should be ordered "on pain of a fine of up to 250,000 euros (£209,000)" not to repeat the claim, and also seeks damages for the impact these statements have made on Patea.
"He was not found guilty, but he was not acquitted and they signed an agreement in which he committed not to talk about this case any more," Patea's lawyer Michael Scheele told BBC Sport.
"Instead he has said that it has been proven that he was not guilty. It's simply false.

"She doesn't want this to be repeated, because she's a content creator, an influencer, and she was accused of trying to make money, which was not true. If that had been the case, she would have asked in that [original] agreement to be compensated.
"He made a payment for the daughter, but nothing for her. She did not get any money."
Zverev is being represented by Berlin law firm Schertz Bergmann, which said: "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit.
"If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings.
"The criminal proceedings were discontinued without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."
The out-of-court settlement in Berlin in June 2024 came on the day Zverev reached the French Open final for the first time.
In the subsequent news conference, he was asked by BBC Sport whether he had any reservations about missing the opportunity to clear his name entirely.
"That's what dropping the case is. That is innocence," Zverev replied.
"They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty. I don't know what translations you have, but that's what it means.
"Done. We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody."

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner
The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.
Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.
You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.
The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford 's Igor Thiago.
In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.
It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton 's James Tarkowski.
Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.
Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United 's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.
But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.
Incident 1: Coventry 's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton 's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.
KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.
What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal 's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City 's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.
KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.
What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."
When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.
The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.
The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.
Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.
KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.
What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."
Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?
KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.
What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."
Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.
KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: England 328 (48.3 overs): Duckett 133, Jacks 59; Edwards 4-31
England confidently swept aside Australia in the third one-day international in Hobart to seal a statement series win.

At times the series decider felt inconsequential - the latest seismic turn in Australia's sandpaper scandal taking all attention during Australia's chase - but Harry Brook's side won by 97 runs in an important step as they build towards next year's World Cup.
Even when failing to fully take advantage of a fast start, England reached 328 before being bowled out in the penultimate over, with Ben Duckett making a fine 133 from 115 balls.

Duckett's century, after all of his struggles in last winter's Ashes, was his first for England on Australian soil. A 48-ball 59 from Will Jacks ensured his innings was not wasted as Australia's spinners slowed scoring through the middle.
Just as impressive was another exciting effort from England's new-ball pair Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker.

Atkinson dismissed Travis Head for the third time in a row in the first over - something to be noted before next year's Ashes series. He also hit Cameron Green with a brutal bouncer that forced the all-rounder to retire hurt.

Baker had Australia captain Mitchell Marsh caught at second slip in the second over, soon added the wicket of Josh Inglis and also dismissed Green's concussion replacement Oliver Peake en route to figures of 4-45.
It helped England calmly close out the win and, after being dismissed for 131 in the series opener, their recovery is noteworthy.
Australia, meanwhile, have questions to ponder on and off the field - many of which are unlikely to be answered before a five-match T20 series begins between these sides on Saturday.

On the field, Australia can at least point to the fact key bowlers – most notably under-fire captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – have been rested for this series as a caveat for their defeat.
On the evidence of this series, England, though inconsistent, look the more settled side.
England had taken strides in ODI cricket this year, beating Sri Lanka (twice) and India, only to be checked by their horror defeats in Pakistan last month. This corrects that course.
Duckett was impressive again but the most significant learning from this series may be the emergence of Baker in partnership with Atkinson.
The 23-year-old Hampshire quick was brought in after defeat in the first ODI and has added real threat with the new ball in his first meeting with Australia.

Bowling has been England's weaker suit in recent ODIs but, given another good start, Liam Dawson was again able to ease through his overs of left-arm spin, bowling Cooper Connolly, having Jack Edwards caught at short fine leg and taking Matt Renshaw caught and bowled with his second ball.

Dropped chances – Baker and Brook put down Renshaw in his 55 and Tom Banton put down a sitter late on – will frustrate, given Brook and the management have spoken of a wish of becoming the best fielding side in the world.

But, after poor run in ODIs which included a failed defence of the World Cup in 2023 and the dismal showing at last year's Champions Trophy, England's 50-over team ends in a much better place than it started.
By having Spencer Johnson caught, Brook even nipped in with the final wicket of the match - his first in ODIs.
Liam Dawson, picked ahead of leg-spinner Adil Rashid, has impressed in this series. 52% of his deliveries would have gone on to hit the stumps
Australia's spinners were more wayward. None of their bowlers had a percentage of deliveries going on to hit the stumps higher than 32%

Duckett, whose difficult Ashes tour last winter included videos of him apparently drunk circulating on social media, averaged 18.33 across 12 previous innings in Australia before this match. His highest score was 42.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic: Carlos Alcaraz was denied a first ATP Finals triumph by Jannik Sinner in last year's final
Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to reach the knockout stage at the ATP Finals.
But the 23-year-old Spaniard later said he had felt "a little problem" with his hamstring.
Alcaraz produced another sparkling display to control the contest throughout, despite ending the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg.
The issue did not disrupt the world number three, who led by a set and a break when he received treatment on the area, as he cruised to a 6-2 6-4 win in just 72 minutes.
"Right now I'm just feeling OK," said Alcaraz, whose qualification for the semi-finals was confirmed by Frances Tiafoe's win against Flavio Cobolli.
"We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me."
It was an 11th consecutive victory for the seven-time major winner, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters.
Alcaraz is scheduled to face Italy's Cobolli - who cannot reach the knockout stage following his 7-6 (8-6) 6-0 loss to Tiafoe - in his final group match in Turin on Friday.
Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: "Everything".
"We could see in [Medvedev's] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep," he added.
"I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I'm really happy about it."
Given the outstanding levels at which he is currently operating, it is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out of action in the middle of the season.
The former world number one's rapid return from that wrist injury to his scintillating best has been astonishing.

Alcaraz has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since making his return at the US Open in August, when his lack of match fitness appeared to catch up with him in a four-and-a-half hour epic against Ben Shelton .
Just 10 weeks on, he delivered one of the best indoor performances of his career in sweeping past 2020 champion Medvedev.
That came two days after he began his latest bid for a first ATP Finals title with a statement victory over Tiafoe - and later warned his rivals he has never felt better at this stage of the season .
Medvedev beat home hope Cobolli in straight sets in his opening match for his first win against a top-10 opponent since defeating Alcaraz at Indian Wells in March.
The Russian was no match for the Australian Open champion on this occasion, however.
A dominant seven-game streak ultimately decided the match, as Alcaraz ran away with the first set and then broke immediately in the second to take firm control.
The second seed did not face a single break point as he outmanoeuvred Medvedev, firing 16 winners and committing just 13 unforced errors.
It was a display which scored 9.5 out of 10 on the ATP's performance rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player's overall game, following a 9.6 in his opener.
That was despite Alcaraz playing the final seven games with the issue in his hamstring, which he will now work to overcome in the next 48 hours.
Frances Tiafoe claimed his sixth win against top-10 opponents in 2026 - the third-most on the tour behind Jannik Sinner (10) and Carlos Alcaraz (eight)
Tiafoe will go head-to-head with Medvedev for a place in the semi-finals after earning his first career win over home favourite Cobolli at the ATP Finals.
The importance of this match to both players' aspirations of progressing on their tournament debut was evident in a tense opening set which featured several momentum swings.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/athletics/ar: The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks.

That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship.

Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is.
There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble.

This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation.
The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat.
"They really help me switch my personality into work mode," he tells BBC Sport. "I think everyone has a work persona and it's a bit more intensified when it comes to my sport.
"Not a lot of things matter when I'm focused on my job, but the rest of the 23 hours and 56-and-a-bit minutes of the day, it's very different."
Kerr is sitting in the bay window of his parents' dining room as the autumnal gloom gathers in this desirable part of Edinburgh. All grand facades, imposing trees and permit parking.
His granny lives at the end of the road. His brother Jake and his family are 20 minutes outside the city. His school – the prestigious George Watson's – is a mile away.

The house has been home since Josh was five months old. Even now, this is where he returns on his five or six trips back to Scotland each year from his Albuquerque base, albeit the "chaos" of his teenage bedroom has long since been vanquished.

"It brings all different sorts of emotions," Kerr says of walking back through the terraced property's teal front door at the start of each visit. "As a kid, I would train from here every day. Everything started from that door.
"It's nice to fall back into that routine when I'm here. I can see the splits I'm running in my loops versus when I was 15. Slightly quicker..."

Around him in the room, pictures of the two brothers fight for space with memorabilia from their careers and assorted artwork. Jake - like their father John - was a professional rugby player, earning a cap for Scotland in the 2019 Six Nations.
He is 18 months older so served as not just an example to follow, but also a target to catch when Josh started racing at the age of nine, having caught the eye at a summer camp.
"If anyone ever wants to nerd out on the family stats, Jake has a pretty awesome under-15 cross-country record," Kerr says.

"We raced a couple of times, once at the Scottish cross-country relays when I ran under someone else's name because they didn't turn up, which was very hush-hush. I just followed him around, holding on for dear life.
"He still likes to remind me that I've never had an unbeaten season and he has. He still thinks he can beat me. That's the solid Kerr delusion in him. But it got me this far, so I can't question it."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Mudryk joined Chelsea in a deal worth up to £89m in January 2023
On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the administration of the Ukraine national team for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football.

The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea , was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, which he believes entered his system while on international duty.
Having initially faced a four-year ban from the Football Association (FA), his appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport was successful.
He returned to football after accepting he had breached anti-doping rules and agreeing to a suspension equivalent to the time he had already served.
After appearing for Chelsea during a pre-season tour of Asia, Mudryk joined Tottenham on transfer deadline day to reunite with his former Shakhtar Donetsk manager Roberto de Zerbi.
In a lengthy interview with the Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk was asked who he blamed for his absence from the game.
"The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team," he replied. "It should never have existed. I probably haven't said it publicly yet, but I'm saying it now.
"I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England."
He explained how he had only been in Ukraine to be with the national team and "it points to the fact it was in a national team camp".
Asked specifically whether he blamed the national team, Mudryk replied: "Yes, exactly."

He also said Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko offered little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and claimed its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
Mudryk also said he spent millions of pounds on legal fees, coaching, pitch hire and private physiotherapy while being unable to access services at Chelsea .
He added: "It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn't believe it [the positive test] was true.
"It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally."
Mudryk said he cried and drank alcohol after the initial suspension but never doubted that he would eventually return to top-level football.
Last year a UAF spokesperson told BBC Sport it was "in close contact with Mudryk's lawyers" but had not been contacted by the FA about the case.

The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first .
But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.
Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.
With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.
Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.
BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.
It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day .
Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.
Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?
Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.
A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.
Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.
Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.
This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".
Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.
It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.
Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.
In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.
In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.
In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.
So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.
Football fans give their thoughts on the Saturday 3pm TV blackout
The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.
The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.
There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.
Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art: Valtteri Bottas has twice finished as a runner-up in the drivers' championship
Valtteri Bottas has been retained by Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season.
The future of the 37-year-old Finn had been in doubt as the American team endure a difficult maiden campaign.
To date, they have failed to collect a point in either the drivers' or constructors' championship.
However, two-time championship runner-up Bottas will race again with them next year.
"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027," said Bottas, who is preparing for Sunday's Las Vegas Grand Prix.
"We knew building a new Formula One team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come. I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."
The news follows the recent announcement that Mexican Sergio Perez, 36, will also be remaining with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a contract extension.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2671614: If there is a more provocative head coach in international rugby these days - apart from South Africa's Rassie Erasmus , obviously - it may be Eddie Jones, the former England boss who predicted the All Blacks' response to their defeat against Wales will be "violent".

Australian Jones, who made his comments in his position as current head coach of Japan following his side's thrashing at the hands of England at Twickenham at the weekend, also used the words "hard", "tough" and "physical" to describe what may be coming from the All Blacks against the English on Sunday morning NZT.
"Well, they're [New Zealand] violent after a defeat," he said. "They're usually violent, very physical. They'll be massively disappointed with that performance [in Cardiff].
"New Zealand next week, they'll be back to the old New Zealand. They'll be hard and tough, and physical around the breakdown."

Days later, an English newspaper reporter was presumably hopeful of having that theme confirmed by All Blacks assistant coach Mike Blair, when he said: "Statistically, there have only been two times in the professional era when New Zealand have lost twice in a row to North Hemisphere opposition.

"With the fact that it was an historic defeat against Wales at the weekend and that you've all said it hurts a lot, how does that come out in the team? Are they going to be really fired up on Saturday? Angry?"

Blair, a former Scotland international halfback now in charge of the All Blacks' attack, metaphorically kicked the question to touch when he replied: "We'll be really focused. We'll have real intent around the game plan and our execution of skills and how we build pressure on England."

Earlier, the same reporter asked Blair how the coaches would attempt to energise an All Black side nearing the end of a rugby year which included a gruelling tour of South Africa and the disappointment of a first loss to Wales since 1953 .
"They're playing for the All Blacks and that's motivation enough," Blair replied. "On top of that you've got how we bounce back from the performance and result against Wales."
The team's fans may hope the All Blacks' response at Twickenham will be similarly businesslike, if not clinical and with few niceties.
The lack of a ruthless streak and a shocking inability to think clearly under pressure in Cardiff were both costly last weekend.

But if we can assume that complacency will not be an issue at a place where they were poor 12 months ago in losing to England , a defeat which was almost certainly the final straw in terms of Scott Robertson's reign as head coach , the mindset at least should be very different. Whether it contains "violence" remains to be seen.

The personnel will certainly be changed, with wing Will Jordan still a possibility to start following his recovery from a hamstring tear and the returns of Ethan de Groot, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie and Jordie Barrett all but inevitable.
There is also the not insignificant matter of Beauden Barrett's potential 150th test - a milestone that will leave him only three short of All Blacks record-holder Sam Whitelock.
Barrett had a difficult time in captaining New Zealand for the first time in a test last weekend and the players around him may feel he is owed a more appropriate tribute on Sunday.
Prop Fletcher Newell sat out training at the All Blacks' base in leafy south-west London overnight but is likely to play.

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.
Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.
The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.
"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.
"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."
Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.
It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'
"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."
But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.
Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.
Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.
And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.
"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.
"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."
"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

World Rugby has banned the 54-year-old for six games for his post-match comments after South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France last weekend, in which he questioned whether officials were manipulating the game.
Erasmus, who has a long track record of publicly criticising match officials , believes they failed to notice, or ignored, up to 17 illegal tackles in Paris.

Hip tackles (a defender putting his weight on the lower limbs of an attacker in the act of bringing him down), and knee tackles (a defender starting the act of making a tackle while on one or both of his knees) was made illegal by World Rugby on 1 November.
All Blacks wing Leroy Carter required ankle surgery after being caught in a hip tackle during his team's Bledisloe Cup victory at Eden Park in October.

"If he saw it and he decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game?"
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus will miss this weekend's test against Ireland.

South Africa Rugby has confirmed Erasmus will request a full misconduct hearing in order to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

The All Blacks also believe some illegal tackles went unpunished in last Sunday's 35-28 loss to Wales in Cardiff, with stand-in captain Beauden Barrett heard on multiple occasions asking referee Pierre Brousset about the hosts making hip drop tackles.
However, All Blacks hooker Asafo Aumua, speaking ahead of his side's clash with England at Twickenham on Sunday, said officials were largely getting it right.
"I think there were a few missed ones on the weekend, but that wasn't going to really change the result in the game," Aumua said.
"I feel like they're [match officials] doing enough, we've just got to be a bit more accurate in our tackles."
Aumua said he didn't think players intentionally made hip or knee drop tackles, but added they could be hard to avoid in a sport as dynamic as rugby.
"On the weekend, I felt like I'd nearly done maybe two [hip drop tackles], but not on purpose," Aumua said.
"I just got beaten on the outside and grabbed them and ended up swinging around, so I just let go."
Aumua said the best way to minimise illegal tackles was to focus on technique.
"Just getting in front [of the attacker] and trying to get them going back instead of swinging around."
As it stands, Erasmus is set to miss the Springboks clash with Ireland this Sunday and their Nations Championship playoff match the following weekend.
The ban is set to expire during next year's Rugby Championship, meaning Erasmus will be back in the hot seat in time for their World Cup title defence in Australia, which starts next October.

Analysis: It may or may not come as a surprise to many global rugby fans to learn that South Africa has a shortage of home-grown referees operating at the top level of the world game.
The nation is the home of the back-to-back world champions and the Springboks are favourites to win every game they play.
And yet, the men and women with the whistles are not coming through in the numbers that represent the extraordinary depth of playing talent 'Boks coach Rassie Erasmus has at his disposal.
Yes, that Rassie Erasmus - the one who has just been banned again by World Rugby under the organisation's "match official abuse sanction process".
His latest suspension is for six matches , including the 'Boks' next Nations Championship test against Ireland in Dublin on Sunday, and the following weekend's play-off at Twickenham.

World Rugby's latest sanction on the game's most prolific agent provocateur comes after his comments in a press conference during which he suggested some of the match officials overseeing South Africa's defeat to France in Paris at the weekend could be accused of "match fixing" such was their determination to avoid penalising what he described as the home side's illegal tackling.
Erasmus has previously been banned for criticising referees - most notably Australian official Nic Berry in 2021 after a defeat to the British and Irish Lions in South Africa.
In that case he filmed a 62-minute rant about what he felt were Berry's shortcomings and posted it on social media.
Berry, who described it as a "character assassination", has not officiated in South Africa since.
Erasmus and his South African Rugby employers have appealed the latest sentence and have requested a right of reply.
France wing Theo Attissogbe scores against South Africa during his team's recent win in Paris.

It is becoming increasingly clear though for all his protestations of innocence that Erasmus doesn't so much carry a rugby nation on his shoulders as whisk his many fervent supporters along in a permanent state of victimhood.

Erasmus can do very little wrong in the eyes of his acolytes; a quick scroll of social media will make that clear, although there is a sense among the more self-aware that while his complaints were valid his suggestions that "match-fixing" was at play may have clouded his argument somewhat.

It wasn't so long ago that Erasmus took great umbrage at suggestions by All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie that the 'Boks' occasionally went beyond the game's scrummaging laws to gain an advantage at the set piece.
"We're not f***ing walking around," was Erasmus' response in August after his team levelled the "Greatest Rivalry" series 1-1 with a victory in Cape Town.
"We're scrumming through. So, you know, we have never ever, ever been accused of walking around. So, I don't understand it."

In that case, according to Erasmus, the match officials were very much right to reward South Africa's scrum dominance and Rennie was very much wrong to air his opinion on a specific topic. Case closed.
World Rugby turned a blind eye or ear to the press conference "F-bomb" - there was no official response anyway.
South Africa are awarded a scrum free-kick during their win over the All Blacks in Baltimore in September.

But the organisation could not fail to act on Erasmus' latest outburst, although one wonders whether the fact that it came in the city which houses World Rugby's headquarters and in front of Northern Hemisphere journalists contributed to the urgency.
