https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8p3: Special Protection Areas are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew
An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.
The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).
Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".
SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.
The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.
The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.
A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.
It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.
It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.
Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.
Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62: Firefighter Steve Williams, pictured here with his widow Jilska, died of a rare lung cancer 14 years after falling into a toxic lagoon
It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.
Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".
Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.
It took 60 firefighters about 18 hours to bring the 1980 fire at Llwyneinion lagoon under control
A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.
Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"
Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
This is the last family photo of Jilska and Steve Williams, with their children David and Kelly, taken in June 1994, shortly before he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer
They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.
They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.
Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.
The 1980 fire at a lagoon used as a dumping site for chemicals was fought for two days.
Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.
"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."
The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer - small cell carcinoma , external - and given weeks to live.
Footage from a BBC news report in August 1980 shows the extent of the toxic waste dump fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon
He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.
The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.
The BBC has been investigating whether discharges of treated sewage might be responsible for poor water quality at a bathing site in Taunton.

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites.
The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.
So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.
We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.
Despite the high levels of faecal bacteria and the health warnings, Jenny, Jo and Jo have kept swimming at the bathing site in Taunton
Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.
The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.
As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.
We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.
That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.
Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.
Last year the official advice was not to swim at 12 of the 14 inland river bathing sites in England .

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?
In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg: Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient

Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.

The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".

"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.

When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
More and more households are installing solar panels, as seen here in Karachi, but Pakistanis still need energy from the national grid
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.

Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89: The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved in 2025.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly: Watch: William and Catherine walk green carpet in Mumbai for Earthshot Prize
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."
William and Catherine talk with guests during the awards ceremony in Mumbai
The royal couple also spoke to those performing, which included Take That
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.
Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: A single meteor streaks across the starry night sky during the annual Leonid meteor shower
The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak on Tuesday night, giving UK sky gazers their best chance to see it this year.
The celestial spectacle runs until 30 November, but the greatest activity is expected on the night of Tuesday 17 November, into the early hours of Wednesday.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the peak. The Moon will set at around 23:30 GMT on Tuesday, meaning its reflected light is less likely to spoil the view in the hours after midnight.
The best chance of seeing the Leonids will be in the far north of Scotland, including Orkney and Shetland, where cloud is expected to be well broken with only a small chance of a passing shower.
Parts of Northern Ireland, Wales, the Midlands and southern England will also have clear spells at times but there will be periods of cloudier weather and some splashes of rain.
In Northern Ireland, the Midlands and North Wales, the best chance of clear breaks will be earlier in the night.
Much of Scotland away from the far north, and northern England, will have limited opportunities. A few places may see the odd gap in the cloud but for most it will be cloudy and damp.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/268090: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/health/2680905%2Fexplainer-the-us-has-lost-its-measles-elimination-status-could-new-zealand
Explainer - More than 25 years ago, the United States effectively stopped measles transmission. This week, it lost its elimination status . How did this happen and could it happen here?
Cases of measles, one of the most contagious viruses there is , have been surging in many countries since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Despite several outbreaks of measles here in New Zealand the past few years, we achieved the elimination of endemic measles cases in October 2017.
US Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

"Measles elimination status" doesn't mean the virus is completely absent, but that a country has interrupted continuous transmission and has a handle on keeping any smaller new outbreaks from spreading.
But that could be at risk as on-time childhood vaccination rates with the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine continue to fall in Aotearoa .
It was officially announced this week that the United States has lost the measles elimination status it achieved in 2000.

The Pan American Health Organisation or PAHO, a division of the World Health Organisation or WHO, confirmed on Tuesday that the United States, along with Bolivia and Mexico, lost their status "as free from endemic measles transmission, as the virus had circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months".

Ambra Hawksley holds her son Andrik Hawksley, age 6, while his sister JaeLynn holds his hand as he prepares to get an MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio, at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas.
"My first reaction is that this was preventable," said Dr Heather Battles, a senior lecturer in anthropology at the University of Auckland who researches infectious disease, epidemics and pandemics.
"The Covid-19 pandemic did interrupt a lot of routine vaccinations, and not just in the US, so there's been a lot of catching up to do," she said.
"And perhaps there hasn't been the political will to invest in public health to do that work."
Measles cases have been steadily on the rise in the US, with outbreaks in largely unvaccinated communities. The disease is highly contagious and can cause serious and life-long health problems .
Some 7700 people in the US have been infected with measles ⁠and 13 have died since 2025, Reuters has reported.
Among them were several children, including a child in New York who died this month and was the state's first death from the disease in 30 years.
"It's a giant stain on our reputation," Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Centre at the Brown University School of Public Health, told The New York Times.
"Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost."
This picture released from UNICEF Samoa shows a girl receiving a vaccine during a nationwide campaign against measles in the Samoan town of Le'auva'a.
If measles spreads continuously for at least 12 months, it meets PAHO's criteria for the return of endemic transmission.
According to WHO, it doesn't mean that the US has lost "all capacity to control the disease" or that it's spreading in wild outbreaks throughout the country. But it is circulating widely.

But it "is a significant public health setback because it means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalisation and death," the Pan American Health Organisation said.

At its peak, 1500 horses and their riders performed in show jumping, dressage and eventing across many disciplines for 55,000 spectators.

"To wind up Horse of the Year (Hawke's Bay) Ltd decision was made at the beginning of the year, if not earlier, so it's been a long time."

The Companies Register showed Horse of the Year (Hawke's Bay) Limited, started in 2012, was overdue in its obligation to file its annual return, so the process to remove the company from the registry was initiated by the Registrar of Companies.
Aitken said he had requested documents from the shareholders to complete the dissolution of the company, but was waiting to hear back.

He said it may have been able to make a modest profit if this year's event went ahead, to cover a loss in 2025, but it was unable to secure funding, including from the district council's events fund to attempt it.

"He'd responded well to treatment, and so he came back because he'd been given the all-clear, which is why we thought 'wow, we've had the miracle'."

"That was his version ot taking it easy. Unfortunately, just due to some complications in hospital... he collapsed, and that was that."

Kwansing said he would be remembered as an intellectual, quiet and reserved, but warm and approachable.
"Not a big talker ... but he was always very direct, articulate, I mean he knew his stuff," she said.
"He [was] very thorough, definitely a subject matter expert all across, and well versed, not just across the economics of the country, but overall geopolitics and all of that."
New Zealand's caretaker Foreign Minister Winston Peters paid tribute to Dr Toatu, describing him as a dedicated champion for the interests of his people.
"We were honoured to spend time with Dr Toatu during our visit to Kiribati earlier this year," he wrote on X.

She recalled her late colleague's heavy influence in the Pacific as a whole, and his status as a statesman creating an atmosphere of trust among leaders.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/country/26731: Scientists in Marlborough are trialling a new way to turn wine and aquaculture industry waste into high-quality protein for animal feed .
A three-year pilot will test whether black soldier flies can convert organic waste like grape marc into protein that can be used in fish and pet food.
The $2.6 million project is being led by the Marlborough Research Centre, with support from the Bioeconomy Science Institute and has received $1.42m in funding from the Waste Minimisation Fund.

Bioeconomy Science Institute business manager Abby Albright said Marlborough's viticulture, aquaculture and fisheries industries produced large volumes of organic waste, and researchers had spent the past five years investigating whether it could be turned into a high-quality insect diet .
The project was focused on the black soldier fly, which Albright said was the "most widely farmed insect globally" because it grew "super, super fast".
She said globally, there was a significant feed protein shortage, but also an emerging insect agriculture sector.

"There's a real opportunity here for us to underpin the quite ambitious growth trajectory of our aquaculture sector, and we can do that in a really beautiful circular way by rearing insects off of the side streams out of the wine making and fisheries sectors."
She said the juvenile insects used in the pilot would come from a Bioeconomy Science Institute research colony in Palmerston North.

The insect farming operation wouldn't have lots of winged insects flying around and the black soldier fly had no chewing mouth parts. Instead, young larvae would be mixed in with a slurry of organic matter and in less than two weeks, they would reach harvestable size, be separated out, dried and milled into a high-protein product.

Albright said once the pilot facility was running at capacity, it was hoped the insects could process 250 kilograms of organic material per day, resulting in around nine tonne of insect biomass, per year.
The leftover product, uneaten food, insect shells and excrement, was called frass, a nutrient-dense product that scientists were also exploring options for.

"It's got a great nutrient profile, it's nitrogen rich and it's also got a really low bulk density so it actually increases the water holding capacity of the soil that it's added to, so we'll be looking at how we can also create a value line item from the frass as well."
Christchurch-based company Kōrure would be responsible for raising, feeding and processing the black solider fly larvae out of two shipping containers in Marlborough.

Founder Ron Park said one container would be used as a fly farm nursery, and the other used to process the waste material. It would run alongside an anaerobic digestion facility managed by bioenergy and waste-to-energy company Ecogas.
Park said the insects would be able to process one tonne of organic waste per week. He said the biggest challenge would be ensuring consistent organic waste across the different seasons.

"Grape marc in summer versus winter will look really, really different so we'll have to mix grape marc with mussel or salmon farm waste to make sure the protein and other nutrient levels are balanced and optimal for the insects."
Park said given the majority of feed stock used in New Zealand was imported, the pilot presented huge opportunities.

"For our country to be able to produce our own protein source for our animals, I believe that's priceless. I'm very excited and very determined to make this work so that we can have a true circular economy here in New Zealand.

An international law expert says it was undiplomatic of the US ambassador to criticise Auckland's mayor .

On Wednesday afternoon, Jared Novelly took to social media to label Wayne Brown a "boomer" and question his intelligence after Brown declared "democracy's had its day" , following a trip to communist China.
Waikato University professor Al Gillespie said there was merit in the comments the ambassador made about Brown and his criticism was fair.
However, he said Novelly should not have done so in a public way, but should have instead made his annoyance clear through the usual diplomatic channels.

"When he speaks, he's speaking not just as an individual, he's speaking as a country and so what people feel is the weight of America in those comments. That that does not help the relationship between the countries when we start to get involved in each other's internal affairs.
"We (New Zealand) try very hard not to say undue things about other countries when New Zealand's got interests, that would be offensive, or interfere and we just need the same respect."
He says the US and Chinese ambassadors were increasingly willing to interfere in New Zealand's domestic affairs.

Gillespie said a recent example of how New Zealand took its diplomatic obligations seriously was the sacking of Phil Goff as New Zealand's High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, because of his comments about US President Donald Trump.
Otago University China foreign policy expert Associate Professor Nicholas Khoo said Brown was ill-informed and didn't understand the complexities of international politics.
His comments were "problematic because they're simply inaccurate".
The US operated within a capitalist system just like China, he said, and it was odd and factually untrue to state otherwise.
While democracy had experienced "some issues" in recent years, he agreed with former UK wartime leader Winston Churchill's assessment: It was the worst system until you considered the alternatives.
Brown also suggested Five Eyes was a waste of time and New Zealand should sell its membership to Japan.

Khoo disagreed: "Mayor Brown is not particularly informed on these issues," which was concerning given his role as mayor of the largest city in the country and a person able to influence public opinion.
"So this is something for us to reflect on and perhaps even consider whether we need more basic understanding of the virtues of capitalism and democracy and also our security alignments."
He added that both democracy and capitalism had worked well for New Zealand and its allies.
Brown, who has been visiting China for 20 years, would have been on a business-related tour stage-managed by the Chinese government, Khoo said.
Brown should have his "eyes open" because it was obvious his comments would be used by the Chinese for propaganda purposes, he said.

"He needs to be much more clued in and for someone who likes to think he's clued in with things it is surprising he's making these sorts of less than tactful comments and certainly were not reflecting the realities and complexities of international politics in the current era."

Pukapuka and Nassau, two remote islands located more than 1100km from Rarotonga, remain under a gale warning, with a strong wind warning still in place for Manihiki and Rakahanga.
Suwarrow, which is an uninhabited, low-lying coral atoll, is under a tropical cyclone alert.
Xavier's maximum sustained winds have dropped to about 175km/h.
The Fiji Meteorological Service's forecast track for the storm shows it is set to drop to a category 3 system in the next 12 hours, and pass just south of Nassau over the coming days.
In its last update on Wednesday night, Emergency Management Cook Islands urged communities across the Northern Cook Islands to remain vigilant and maintain a heightened state of preparedness.
"The cyclone's very slow movement may prolong adverse weather and coastal hazards across the affected islands," it said.
Meanwhile, the Cook Islands government has accepted New Zealand's offer to deploy two rapid response team personnel to assist with humanitarian coordination and emergency operations.

"It was confirmed that as of 8pm yesterday (local time), the two experienced personnel from New Zealand's Rapid Response Team arrived to support with liaising with the NZ defence personnel if required," Cook Islands News reported.
The newspaper said more than 300 people were evacuated to a cyclone shelter on Pukapuka on Monday (Tuesday NZDT) when Xavier reached category 5 status.

"On Pukapuka, residents spent the night at the cyclone shelter, with families returning to their homes [Tuesday] morning to collect belongings, secure loose building materials and make further preparations before returning to the shelter," it reported.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regions_cante: An independent review has uncovered widespread weaknesses in Selwyn District Council's historic water billing system, estimating almost $3 million may have gone unbilled, while the full financial extent remains unclear.

The PwC report estimated about $2.87m might not have been billed between 1 July 2024 and 31 December 2025. It identified about 1300 properties with missing or incorrect billing records, and about 2200 records where billing started later than it should have.

The review separately identified 809 meters showing water consumption without an associated billing account. PwC could not calculate how much revenue might have been missed because sufficient historic meter readings were unavailable.
Selwyn District Council chief executive Steve Gibling said the report showed where the council fell short.
"We accept what the review found. I'm making putting it right my top priority, and that work has already begun," he said.
"Importantly, if you've had a bill from Selwyn Water, the amount on it is correct. This means everyone is now paying their fair share for the water they use.

"What we've identified is that the connection between our property valuation data, the meter reading data and our systems weren't adequately connected and more importantly they weren't being regularly tested to make sure they're producing consistent results. That's one of the things our team have put in place now to rectify this."

The report looked at drinking water charges from 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2025, and wastewater charges over the 18 months to 30 June 2026. The periods reviewed all fell before 1 July 2026, when water services moved to Selwyn Water Limited.
Mayor Lydia Gliddon stressed that no one would be sent a backdated bill.
"The time available to correct any undercharging through the Rating Act has passed. We also don't think it would be fair when the mistakes were in council's own systems," she said.

PwC said where the council decided not to recover historic amounts, it should consider fairness to customers who were correctly charged, "including whether unrecovered historic amounts may ultimately be borne by other current or future customers or ratepayers".

Gliddon said the council did not regard the historic underbilling as a budget shortfall that had to be recovered from other customers or ratepayers, because the revenue had not been included in its budget.

"The first thing to recognise is that this is unbilled revenue, it's unbudgeted, unbilled. They kind of do cancel each other out from us on the Selwyn District Council side of things and is historical. The billing coming out of Selwyn Water is true and accurate now," she said.

In terms of the 809 meters that could not be matched to a billing account and the potential revenue associated with them, Gliddon said the council expected to have a clearer picture before the end of the financial year.

"[Selwyn Water is] quantifying all that information and that's exactly why we asked for a one-year water services strategy so that they could look at quantifying all that information, looking at what the actual revenue take should be before they even work on a 10-year outlook," she said.

The review also found 70 trade waste consent holders could not be linked to current trade waste billing records, while 340 businesses in industries commonly associated with trade waste were not clearly represented in the consent or billing records. PwC could not quantify any potential missing revenue because the required historical information was unavailable.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/bee-swarm: Auckland is seeing about twice as many bee swarms as usual this spring, with local beekeepers getting up to 10 calls for help a day.
Ken Brown, president of the Auckland Beekeepers Club, said the milder winter was the reason. He said the swarms had started about four weeks earlier than normal.
A swarm happens when a hive gets too crowded. The bees raise a new queen, and the old queen flies off with up to half the colony to start a new home somewhere else.
Brown said this is natural and “a sign of a good, strong, healthy hive”. In one backyard, thousands of bees turned up at once.

Phil Lester, a biology professor at Victoria University, said bees had been breeding well and growing their numbers. He said bees are important because they pollinate many of the crops we grow for food.
Swarms are being spotted all over New Zealand, and experts think swarming season could last until January.
Brown said swarms are not much of a risk to people, even if they can be a surprise to see in the city.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/des-bucki: New Zealand Football has confirmed Des Buckingham as the new head coach of the All Whites, New Zealand’s men’s football team, starting on 1 July 2027 and continuing through to the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

He is not new to New Zealand football. Buckingham lived and worked here for seven years, including as an assistant coach with the All Whites and head coach of the Men’s Under-23 side. In 2019, he guided that team to qualification for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and to New Zealand’s first-ever Pacific Games football gold medal.
That same year, he led the Men’s Under-20 team to the country’s highest-ever finish at a men’s FIFA World Cup tournament, including a record 5-0 win over Honduras.

Since then, Buckingham has coached around the world, most recently as head coach of Al-Kholood in Saudi Arabia. He also led English club Oxford United into the Championship division for the first time in 25 years.
New Zealand Football chief executive Andrew Pragnell said the appointment was a big moment for the sport.
“I’m incredibly proud to announce Des as the new All Whites Coach,” Pragnell said. “This is huge for New Zealand Football and the future success of both NZF and the All Whites.”
Fans will have to wait until next July to see Buckingham take charge.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/new-parki: From December, visitors will have to pay to park at some of New Zealand’s most popular outdoor spots, as the Department of Conservation (DOC) rolls out paid parking more widely.
Sites getting paid car parks include Goat Island north of Auckland, the Tasman Glacier, Kura Tāwhiti/Castle Hill, the Routeburn Divide, and the Kepler Track control gates, among others.

At most of these places, the cost will be $2.50 for every half hour, or $20 for the whole day. At Goat Island, the first 10 minutes are free for quick drop-offs and pick-ups, and there is a separate $15 daily rate over winter.

People who live nearby can buy a $10 annual permit instead, which covers unlimited parking all year for up to two vehicles. School groups, DOC volunteers and community groups will be able to apply for an exemption.
The new fees follow a trial that started in the South Island earlier this year, at places like Punakaiki’s Pancake Rocks, Franz Josef and Aoraki Mount Cook.
David Butt, DOC’s director of heritage and visitors, said the money raised, expected to be about $3 million over the next year, would help look after the sites.
“We will use paid parking to generate revenue to contribute to the long-term care of places like Goat Island,” he said.

Cameras will keep track of cars coming in and out, and anyone who doesn’t pay could be issued a $75 breach notice – so if your family is planning a summer trip to one of these spots, it might pay to bring some extra coins.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/robert-pa: British actor Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the famous spy in the 64-year-old film series.

The Bond films, based on novels by Ian Fleming, have earned more than US$7 billion at the box office since the first film in 1962. Fans will have to wait a while yet to see Pattinson in action as 007.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/christmas: Santa Claus is gearing up for a busy few weeks, with more than 30 Christmas parades, markets and festivals planned across Auckland this November and December.
Local boards are putting in more than $400,000 to help fund the events, though most of the money is coming from businesses and donations rather than ratepayers.

Some organisers say money has been tighter this year. The team behind the Howick Santa Parade, which rolls through the suburb on 13 December, said they were working with a smaller budget than usual, and it had been harder than normal to find volunteers to help out.
Other parades are pushing ahead with big plans. The Onehunga Santa Parade, set for Saturday 21 November, will have about 40 floats making their way down the street.

Onehunga Business Association manager Victoria Puxty said the parade almost didn’t happen because of funding troubles. “We just didn’t have the funding,” she said. But the community pulled together to make it work anyway. “We managed to do it; it was pretty much 100% voluntary,” she said.
Christmas parades are a loved tradition in many New Zealand towns and cities, with whānau lining the streets to wave at floats, watch dancers and catch lollies thrown from passing trucks.
If you’re keen to catch a parade this year, it’s worth checking your local council’s website to find out exact dates and road closures near you.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/why-nzs-e: New Zealanders might still be waiting for a final election result, but experts say that’s no reason for political parties to sit on their hands.
New Zealand held its general election recently, but because of how the voting system works, it takes about 20 days to count every vote and declare a final result.

Constitutional law expert Graeme Edgeler said the wait isn’t really about “special votes” — the votes cast by people overseas, outside their electorate, or enrolled close to election day. Instead, he said, it’s about making sure the count is completely accurate.
Chief electoral officer Karl le Quesne agreed. “We take a great deal of care to make sure it’s complete and accurate, so people can trust the result,” he said.

Edgeler pointed out that political parties don’t have to wait for the final numbers before they start talking to each other about forming a government. He said there’s “nothing stopping politicians from starting their negotiations now.” Back in 2008, John Key’s first government was sworn in before the final vote count had even finished.
Because of how New Zealand’s MMP voting system works, Parliament is expected to end up with 131 seats this time, a few more than the usual 120, because of something called an “overhang”.
For now, Kiwis will just have to be patient while the votes are carefully checked and counted.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/philippin: A 19-year-old singer from the Philippines has won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, held in Bangkok, Thailand, on Saturday 14 November 2026.

CARMELLE took out the brand-new competition with her song “Sobra-Sobra”, performing at the Grand Final held at the One Bangkok Forum. This is the first time Eurovision, usually held in Europe, has launched a sister contest especially for Asian countries.
Artists from 11 different countries took part, singing in 10 different languages as well as English, all under the theme “United by Music”.

CARMELLE finished with 211 points in total: 93 points from judging panels in each country, and 118 points from members of the public who voted. People in 183 countries and territories around the world were able to vote for their favourite performance, with the public vote making up half of the final result.
Thailand came second with 170 points, and Vietnam placed third with 164 points. Malaysia and Laos rounded out the top five.

Martin Green, Director of the Eurovision Song Contest, congratulated the winner. “Congratulations to CARMELLE and the Philippines on becoming the first-ever winners of Eurovision Song Contest Asia,” he said.
Organisers hope the contest will return next year, giving more Asian performers the chance to shine on a huge stage.
